meta.title: AIF Hard Quiz 7
meta.focus: real-time vs serverless · underfitting · ML types · sampling settings · fine-tune vs RAG · governance look-alikes

questions.scenario: A ride-hailing company runs a pricing model that receives thousands of requests every second, all day and night. Each price must be returned in less than 50 milliseconds, and even a short delay while the endpoint wakes up is not acceptable. Which SageMaker inference option fits BEST?
options: SageMaker real-time inference
SageMaker Serverless Inference with high concurrency
SageMaker Asynchronous Inference with notifications
SageMaker batch transform on a large GPU instance
questions.explain: Steady, very high traffic + milliseconds + no wake-up delay = real-time inference (instances are always running). Serverless is the trap: it scales to zero, so a request after an idle period can hit a cold start, and it suits rare or uneven traffic. Asynchronous puts requests in a queue for long jobs. Batch transform is offline. Trick: Serverless = sleeps when nobody calls; real-time = always awake.

questions.scenario: A team's model has an ERROR of 40% on the training data and 41% on the test data. The team wants to lower both numbers. Which action is MOST likely to help?
options: Use a more complex model and add more useful features
Add stronger regularization so the model stays as simple as possible
Stop training earlier, after fewer epochs
Remove features so the model has less to learn
questions.explain: Careful, this says ERROR. HIGH error on BOTH training and test data = the model has not even learned the training data = underfitting (high bias). Fix: a more complex model, better features or longer training. Regularization, early stopping and removing features all make the model simpler; they fix OVERFITTING and would make this worse. Check: is training error low? No = underfitting.

questions.scenario: A shipping company's model predicts the delivery cost of each parcel in dollars. Managers want one metric, shown in dollars, that punishes a few very large mistakes more strongly than many small ones. Which metric fits BEST?
options: Root mean squared error (RMSE)
Mean absolute error (MAE)
F1 score
Area under the ROC curve (AUC)
questions.explain: A dollar number = regression. Punishes large mistakes more = RMSE, because each error is squared before averaging, and the square root brings the result back to dollars. MAE is the trap: it is also in dollars, but every dollar of error counts the same. F1 and AUC are for classification (categories), not numbers.

questions.scenario: Match each business task to the type of machine learning that fits it.
options: Clustering (unsupervised learning)
Self-supervised learning
Regression (supervised learning)
Classification (supervised learning)
questions.explain: A number (kWh) = regression. Labelled examples + categories = classification. No labels + find groups = clustering. The model makes its own labels from the data (the hidden word is the label) = self-supervised learning, which is how foundation models are pre-trained. Regression and classification are both supervised because they learn from labelled answers.
prompts: Predict tomorrow's electricity use in kilowatt-hours from weather data
Put news articles into 'sport', 'politics' or 'business' using thousands of articles that people have already tagged
Find natural groups of shoppers when no groups or labels exist
Pre-train a language model by hiding words in billions of untagged sentences and predicting them

questions.scenario: A team turns each of its 50,000 support articles into a list of 1,024 numbers. Articles with similar meaning get lists that are close together, even when they use different words. What are these lists of numbers called?
options: Vector embeddings
Token IDs from the tokenizer
Model weights (parameters)
Attention scores from the transformer
questions.explain: Numbers that capture MEANING, where similar meanings sit close together = embeddings (vectors). They are stored in a vector database for semantic search and RAG. Token IDs are just numbers for pieces of words, with no meaning distance. Model weights are what a model learns in training. Attention scores exist inside the model while it processes one input.

questions.scenario: During testing, a developer sets top-k to 1 for a text model on Amazon Bedrock. What is the MOST likely effect on the output?
options: The model always picks the single most likely next token
The model's answer is cut down to one sentence only
The model picks from the words that make up the top 1% of probability
The model returns only one answer instead of several options
questions.explain: Top-k = choose the next token from only the k most likely ones. With k = 1 there is only one choice, so output becomes very predictable. Answer length is set by max tokens, not top-k. 'Top 1% of probability' describes top-p, which uses a probability share, not a count. Trick: top-K = a fixed count (K words); top-P = a Percentage of probability.

questions.scenario: A transformer model reads the sentence 'The bank by the river was flooded'. To understand that 'bank' means the side of a river and not a place for money, the model checks how each word relates to every other word in the sentence. Which part of the transformer does this?
options: The self-attention mechanism
The tokenizer that splits text into pieces
The temperature setting used during sampling
The context window limit
questions.explain: Weighing how every word relates to every other word = self-attention, the core idea of transformers. The tokenizer only splits text into tokens. Temperature controls how random the word choice is. The context window is how much text fits, not how meaning is worked out.

questions.scenario: A compliance team needs a Bedrock model to give answers that are as consistent as possible when the same question is asked many times. Which TWO setting changes help MOST? (Select TWO)
options: Lower the temperature to close to 0
Lower top-p to a small value such as 0.1
Raise top-k to 500
Raise the maximum output length
Add a stop sequence to the end of each answer
questions.explain: Consistency = less randomness. Lower temperature and lower top-p both shrink the choice of next words. Raising top-k to 500 does the opposite: more words to choose from. Max output length and stop sequences only control WHERE the answer ends, not which words are chosen.

questions.scenario: An airline has 10,000 past customer messages, each paired with the reply that its best agents sent. It wants a model that always writes replies in this same tone and structure, without long instructions in every prompt. Which approach fits BEST?
options: Fine-tune a foundation model on the message and reply pairs
Build a RAG Knowledge Base from the 10,000 message and reply pairs
Put ten of the replies in every prompt as few-shot examples
Run continued pre-training on the airline's unlabelled website text
questions.explain: Thousands of labelled input + ideal output pairs + a lasting style = fine-tuning. RAG is the trap: it retrieves FACTS at question time, but it does not teach the model a tone, and it makes every prompt longer. Few-shot with ten examples adds tokens to every request and learns less than training on 10,000. Continued pre-training uses unlabelled text to learn a domain's words, not a reply style. Trick: many PAIRS = fine-tune; changing FACTS = RAG.

questions.scenario: A developer writes a prompt with two solved examples: each shows a customer comment and its correct category. Then the prompt gives a new comment and asks for its category. Her manager says, 'So you fine-tuned the model with two records.' Which statement is correct?
options: No. This is few-shot prompting, and the model's weights do not change
Yes. This is fine-tuning, and Bedrock saves the two examples into a custom model
No. This is RAG, because the examples are extra context added to the prompt
No. This is zero-shot prompting, because no training job was started
questions.explain: Examples written inside the prompt = few-shot prompting (two examples = 'two-shot'). Nothing is trained and no weights change. Fine-tuning needs a training job and creates a new custom model. RAG automatically retrieves information from a data source; hand-written examples are not retrieval. Zero-shot means NO examples at all.

questions.scenario: A team is building an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base so its assistant can answer questions from 3,000 PDF manuals stored in Amazon S3. Besides the S3 data source, which TWO components does the Knowledge Base need? (Select TWO)
options: An embeddings model to turn text chunks into vectors
A vector store to save and search those vectors
A labelled dataset of question and answer pairs
Provisioned Throughput for the text generation model
A SageMaker training job to retrain the base model
questions.explain: RAG = turn chunks into embeddings (an embeddings model such as Titan Text Embeddings) and keep them in a vector store (such as OpenSearch Serverless) for similarity search. RAG needs no labelled pairs and no training job, because the base model is never changed. Provisioned Throughput is optional; on-demand works.

questions.scenario: A company uses a model to turn English safety notices into Urdu. Professional translators have already written Urdu versions of 2,000 of these notices. The company wants a standard automatic score that compares the model's output with these human versions. Which metric fits BEST?
options: BLEU
ROUGE
Perplexity
Accuracy
questions.explain: Comparing machine TRANSLATION with human translations = BLEU ('Bilingual'). ROUGE is the trap: it also compares with human text, but it is the standard for short versions of long text (summaries). Perplexity does not use a human reference. Accuracy is for classification, where each answer is simply right or wrong.

questions.scenario: An online shop wants an assistant that, during a chat, checks a customer's order status in the shop's internal order system through an API, and then starts a return if the customer asks for one. Which Amazon Bedrock feature fits BEST?
options: Amazon Bedrock Agents
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation
questions.explain: Take ACTIONS by calling APIs over several steps = Bedrock Agents (action groups). Knowledge Bases only look up documents to answer questions; they cannot start a return. Guardrails filter harmful or off-topic content. Model evaluation compares model quality before launch.

questions.scenario: A chatbot model sometimes repeats real customers' phone numbers that were inside its training data. The team will train a new version next month. Which action BEST prevents this problem in the new version?
options: Find and remove personal data from the training data before training
Raise the temperature so the model is less likely to repeat exact text
Document the problem in a SageMaker Model Card for the new version
Train the new version for more epochs so it learns general patterns
questions.explain: If personal data is in the training data, the model can memorise and repeat it, so the fix is to clean the data BEFORE training (for example, find it with Amazon Macie in S3, then remove or mask it). Raising temperature does not remove the data. A Model Card records the risk but does not fix it. More epochs increases memorisation.

questions.scenario: A company uses two kinds of AI: Amazon Transcribe, and its own fraud model that it built in SageMaker. Auditors want documentation about the intended use and limitations of both. Which pairing is MOST appropriate?
options: AWS AI Service Card for Transcribe; SageMaker Model Card for the fraud model
SageMaker Model Card for Transcribe; AWS AI Service Card for the fraud model
AWS Artifact report for Transcribe; AWS Audit Manager report for the fraud model
SageMaker Model Card for both, because both models run on AWS
questions.explain: AWS writes AI Service Cards for its OWN services, such as Transcribe. YOU write SageMaker Model Cards for models YOU build. The swapped pair is the trap. Artifact and Audit Manager are compliance tools, not model documentation. You cannot properly document AWS's internal Transcribe model in your own Model Card.

questions.scenario: A company trained a hiring model on ten years of its own past hiring decisions. In those years, managers hired very few women. The new model now gives women lower scores than equally qualified men. What is the MOST likely root cause?
options: Bias in the historical training data
Overfitting caused by too many training epochs
Data drift after the model was deployed
Hallucination caused by a high temperature setting
questions.explain: The model learned the unfair pattern that was already in the past decisions = bias in the training data. Overfitting means good on training data but bad on new data in general, not unfair to one group. Drift is a change AFTER deployment, but this problem existed from the start. Hallucination and temperature are GenAI ideas, not part of a hiring score model.

questions.scenario: Last Tuesday, someone turned off model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock. The security team must find out which IAM user did it, at what time, and from which IP address. Which service provides this information?
options: AWS CloudTrail
Amazon CloudWatch Logs
Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms
AWS Config conformance packs
questions.explain: WHO did WHAT, WHEN and from WHERE (IP address) = a record of an API call = CloudTrail. CloudWatch Logs is the trap: it can store the invocation logs themselves, but the record of who changed the setting is in CloudTrail. CloudWatch metrics track numbers such as latency. Config tracks resource settings and rules, not the caller's IP. Trick: Trail = footprints of who did it; Watch = health and performance.

questions.scenario: An ML team needs two things: (1) a continuous check that every S3 bucket of training data stays encrypted, with a history of when that setting changed, and (2) an alarm when GPU use on its training instances stays above 90% for 15 minutes. Which TWO services meet these needs? (Select TWO)
options: AWS Config
Amazon CloudWatch
Amazon Inspector
Amazon Macie
AWS CloudTrail
questions.explain: (1) Settings checked against a rule, with history = AWS Config. (2) Metrics and alarms = CloudWatch. CloudTrail records who called an API, not whether settings follow a rule. Inspector scans software for CVEs. Macie finds sensitive data in S3.

questions.scenario: A healthcare startup will process patient data with AI services on AWS. Its lawyer needs to review and accept the AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA) for HIPAA. Where can the company do this by itself in the AWS console?
options: AWS Artifact
AWS Audit Manager
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Config
questions.explain: AWS's own agreements and reports (BAA, SOC, ISO) = AWS Artifact; you can review and accept the BAA there yourself. Audit Manager collects evidence about YOUR resources, Trusted Advisor gives best-practice tips, and Config records resource settings. Trick: Artifact = AWS's papers.

questions.scenario: A company fine-tunes a model in Amazon Bedrock. Security rules say the custom model must be encrypted with a key that the company creates and controls, with a key policy it writes, and every use of the key must be logged. Which option fits BEST?
options: A customer managed key in AWS KMS
AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation
An AWS owned key, which is the default
Amazon Macie with automatic sensitive data discovery
questions.explain: Encryption with a key YOU create and control, with your own key policy and CloudTrail records of each use = a KMS customer managed key. Secrets Manager stores secrets such as passwords and API keys; it is not the encryption key for a model. An AWS owned key is the default, but you cannot see, control or audit it. Macie finds sensitive data; it does not encrypt anything.
